welcome_to_module.overview: Children grow and develop in many different ways. Some begin talking earlier, some later. Some are cautious with movement, while others climb and run quickly. Some children enjoy busy groups, while others need more time to feel comfortable. These differences do not automatically mean that anything is wrong.[span_1](start_span)[span_1](end_span)
welcome_to_module.context: At the same time, adults who know children well may notice patterns that deserve closer attention. A parent may notice that a child is not responding to sounds. A teacher may observe that a child struggles to understand simple routines across many days. A caregiver may notice that a child has stopped using words they previously used.[span_2](start_span)[span_2](end_span)
welcome_to_module.purpose: The purpose of this module is not to teach you to diagnose children. It is to help you notice, observe, record, communicate, and seek appropriate guidance.[span_3](start_span)[span_3](end_span)
welcome_to_module.central_message: A developmental concern is not a diagnosis. It is a reason to observe, ask questions, and seek appropriate professional guidance.[span_4](start_span)[span_4](end_span)

what_is_child_development.definition: Child development is the gradual process through which children gain skills, understanding, relationships, and increasing independence. Development happens in many connected areas:[span_6](start_span)[span_6](end_span)
areas: Physical and motor development: Moving the body, sitting, walking, running, balancing, using hands and fingers.[span_7](start_span)[span_7](end_span)
Language and communication: Listening, understanding, gestures, sounds, words, signing, speaking, and sharing ideas.[span_8](start_span)[span_8](end_span)
Cognitive development: Learning, remembering, exploring, solving simple problems, understanding routines, and using imagination.[span_9](start_span)[span_9](end_span)
Social and emotional development: Connecting with others, playing, expressing feelings, responding to comfort, and learning to manage emotions.[span_10](start_span)[span_10](end_span)
Everyday functioning: Eating, dressing, toileting, participating in routines, and doing age-appropriate tasks with support.[span_11](start_span)[span_11](end_span)
what_is_child_development.note: These areas overlap. For example, a child’s ability to join a group activity may be affected by communication, hearing, confidence, movement, sleep, or familiarity with the activity.[span_12](start_span)[span_12](end_span)

what_is_a_developmental_milestone.definition: A developmental milestone is something that most children can do by a certain age. Examples include sitting, pointing, using words, following simple instructions, running, pretending in play, or taking turns.[span_13](start_span)[span_13](end_span)
what_is_a_developmental_milestone.details: Milestones are useful guides. They help adults notice progress and identify questions to discuss. They are not labels, intelligence tests, or diagnoses.[span_14](start_span)[span_14](end_span)
what_is_a_developmental_milestone.important_note: A child who has not reached one milestone at one particular moment is not automatically delayed or disordered. Children develop at different speeds, and some skills emerge gradually rather than appearing suddenly. CDC milestone lists describe skills that most children—at least 75%—can do by the stated age, but the lists are not diagnostic screening tools.[span_15](start_span)[span_15](end_span)

what_is_a_developmental_concern.definition: A developmental concern is an observation that a child may need closer attention, additional support, screening, or professional assessment.[span_16](start_span)[span_16](end_span)
concern_triggers: Is not making expected progress over time.[span_17](start_span)[span_17](end_span)
Has difficulty taking part in everyday activities for their age.[span_18](start_span)[span_18](end_span)
Shows a pattern of concerns in more than one developmental area.[span_19](start_span)[span_19](end_span)
Has lost a skill they previously used.[span_20](start_span)[span_20](end_span)
Has a difference that is persistent, worsening, or affecting wellbeing.[span_21](start_span)[span_21](end_span)
Has a parent, caregiver, teacher, or childcare worker who remains worried.[span_22](start_span)[span_22](end_span)
what_is_a_developmental_concern.note: A concern does not tell us why something is happening. It does not tell us whether a child has a particular condition. It tells us that it is worth learning more.[span_23](start_span)[span_23](end_span)

developmental_variation_versus_concern.developmental_variation: A child reaches a skill somewhat earlier or later than another child but continues to make steady progress[span_24](start_span)[span_24](end_span)
developmental_variation_versus_concern.possible_developmental_concern: A child’s progress has stopped, slowed markedly, or moved backwards[span_25](start_span)[span_25](end_span)

developmental_variation_versus_concern.developmental_variation: A child is shy when first entering a new childcare setting but gradually becomes comfortable[span_26](start_span)[span_26](end_span)
developmental_variation_versus_concern.possible_developmental_concern: A child remains unable to engage or participate over time across familiar settings[span_27](start_span)[span_27](end_span)

developmental_variation_versus_concern.developmental_variation: A child speaks fewer words in one language but communicates meaningfully across the languages used at home[span_28](start_span)[span_28](end_span)
developmental_variation_versus_concern.possible_developmental_concern: A child has persistent difficulty communicating needs, understanding familiar language, or using gestures, sounds, words, or other communication methods across settings[span_29](start_span)[span_29](end_span)

developmental_variation_versus_concern.developmental_variation: A child needs extra practice with stairs, a spoon, crayons, or dressing[span_30](start_span)[span_30](end_span)
developmental_variation_versus_concern.possible_developmental_concern: A child has persistent movement or hand-use difficulties that significantly limit everyday participation[span_31](start_span)[span_31](end_span)

developmental_variation_versus_concern.developmental_variation: A toddler has tantrums when tired, hungry, frustrated, or adjusting to change[span_32](start_span)[span_32](end_span)
developmental_variation_versus_concern.possible_developmental_concern: Emotional distress or behaviour is persistent, severe, or repeatedly prevents play, relationships, learning, or daily routines[span_33](start_span)[span_33](end_span)

why_one_unusual_behaviour_does_not_mean_.explanation: Children have difficult days. They may be tired, hungry, unwell, shy, overstimulated, scared, or adjusting to a new person or environment. A child may refuse to talk to visitors but chat at home. A child may not use a spoon at childcare because they are usually fed at home. A child may not answer a question because they do not understand the language used.[span_34](start_span)[span_34](end_span)
why_one_unusual_behaviour_does_not_mean_.conclusion: One moment is a small piece of information. A pattern observed over time and across settings is more useful.[span_35](start_span)[span_35](end_span)
why_one_unusual_behaviour_does_not_mean_.remember: Remember: Observe first. Ask questions next. Avoid conclusions.[span_36](start_span)[span_36](end_span)

your_role_as_an_observer.overview: Parents, relatives, teachers, childcare workers, and community members may notice changes in a child’s development because they see the child regularly. This is valuable information. However, noticing is not diagnosing.[span_38](start_span)[span_38](end_span)
responsibilities: Pay attention to the child’s strengths and challenges.[span_39](start_span)[span_39](end_span)
Observe what happens in ordinary daily situations.[span_40](start_span)[span_40](end_span)
Share concerns appropriately with the child’s parent or caregiver.[span_43](start_span)[span_43](end_span)
Continue to support the child’s participation and learning.[span_45](start_span)[span_45](end_span)

daily_life_observations: Play with objects, adults, and other children[span_47](start_span)[span_47](end_span)
Understanding and responding to words, gestures, or visual cues[span_53](start_span)[span_53](end_span)
Expressing needs, choices, discomfort, enjoyment, or ideas[span_54](start_span)[span_54](end_span)
Responding to sounds, voices, and visual information[span_55](start_span)[span_55](end_span)
strengths_to_observe: How do they communicate when they want something?[span_59](start_span)[span_59](end_span)
In which settings do they seem most confident?[span_62](start_span)[span_62](end_span)

why_context_matters.overview: A behaviour only makes sense when we understand the situation around it.[span_63](start_span)[span_63](end_span)
questions_to_ask: Was the child tired, hungry, unwell, or recovering from illness?[span_64](start_span)[span_64](end_span)
Was the environment unfamiliar, noisy, crowded, or frightening?[span_65](start_span)[span_65](end_span)
Was the activity too difficult, too easy, or unfamiliar?[span_66](start_span)[span_66](end_span)
Did the child understand the language being used?[span_67](start_span)[span_67](end_span)
Have they had opportunities to practise this skill?[span_68](start_span)[span_68](end_span)
Is the child more comfortable communicating in another language?[span_69](start_span)[span_69](end_span)
Does the child behave differently at home, childcare, school, worship settings, or with relatives?[span_70](start_span)[span_70](end_span)
Was there a recent major change, such as a move, a new sibling, bereavement, family stress, or a new childcare arrangement?[span_71](start_span)[span_71](end_span)

avoid_unfair_comparisons.overview: Comparing children can sometimes provide a general reference point, but it can also create anxiety and shame. Avoid statements such as: "Her younger cousin can already talk better." "All the other children can do it." "Your child is far behind." "He is lazy." "She is stubborn." "He is not intelligent." "She is behaving like a baby.\[span_73](start_span)
avoid_unfair_comparisons.guidance: Children differ in temperament, health, language exposure, opportunities, learning styles, and experiences. Compare a child mainly with their own previous progress, not with the most advanced child around them.[span_74](start_span)[span_74](end_span)

culture_language_and_opportunity.overview: Children grow within families and communities. Development can be influenced by:[span_75](start_span)[span_75](end_span)
influences: The languages used at home and in childcare[span_76](start_span)[span_76](end_span)
Whether adults and children communicate through speech, gesture, sign, pictures, songs, stories, or a combination[span_77](start_span)[span_77](end_span)
Access to books, toys, play spaces, and safe movement opportunities[span_78](start_span)[span_78](end_span)
Whether children are expected to feed or dress themselves at a particular age[span_80](start_span)[span_80](end_span)
Experience with stairs, utensils, crayons, group activities, or peer play[span_81](start_span)[span_81](end_span)
culture_language_and_opportunity.note: Growing up with more than one language does not by itself cause a developmental disorder. Professionals should consider the child’s communication across all languages and communication methods they use. A child’s ability to communicate meaning—not only the number of English words they use—matters.[span_83](start_span)[span_83](end_span)

how_to_document_objectively.overview: Objective documentation describes what you saw or heard without guessing why it happened.[span_84](start_span)[span_84](end_span)

comparisons.more_useful_objective_observation: “During the three-hour morning session, the child used two spoken words: ‘mama’ and ‘ball.’ They also pointed, pulled an adult’s hand toward a cup, and cried when unable to reach an item.[span_86](start_span)”[span_86](end_span)
“When two familiar adults called her name during snack time, she did not turn. When the same adults showed her a favourite toy, she looked toward them.[span_88](start_span)”[span_88](end_span)
“During outdoor play, he pushed another child twice when both reached for the same tricycle. He cried when the tricycle was removed.[span_90](start_span)”[span_90](end_span)
“She followed the routine ‘put your cup on the table’ after watching the other children, but did not respond when the instruction was given without gestures.[span_92](start_span)”[span_92](end_span)
“He fell three times while running on uneven ground and held the railing with both hands when using steps.[span_94](start_span)”[span_94](end_span)

“She played beside other children for 15 minutes and watched them closely. She moved away when another child took her toy. She smiled when a familiar caregiver joined her play.[span_96](start_span)”[span_96](end_span)

how_to_document_objectively.note: Objective notes help healthcare and developmental professionals understand the child’s actual functioning. Labels do not.[span_97](start_span)[span_97](end_span)

format.what_to_record: Home, classroom, outdoor play, meal, clinic, family gathering[span_101](start_span)[span_101](end_span)
Describe visible actions, sounds, gestures, words, and responses[span_105](start_span)[span_105](end_span)
How did the child respond? What support helped?[span_109](start_span)[span_109](end_span)
What could the child do? What did they enjoy?[span_111](start_span)[span_111](end_span)
What do we need to observe or ask next?[span_113](start_span)[span_113](end_span)

a_simple_observation_record.example_observation_note: Date: 12 March. Setting: Childcare centre, morning group time. Observation: During a 10-minute song activity, Musa watched other children and clapped after the teacher demonstrated. When the teacher asked, “Where is your nose?” Musa did not respond. When his caregiver touched her own nose and repeated the question, he smiled and touched his nose. Strength: He copied the clapping and responded to a gesture. Next question: Does he understand familiar words when gestures are not used? Does he respond similarly at home and in his strongest language?[span_114](start_span)[span_114](end_span)

a_careful_approach_to_warning_signs.overview: The phrase “warning sign” can sound frightening. In this module, it means a pattern that may be worth discussing with a qualified professional. It does not mean a child has a diagnosis.[span_116](start_span)[span_116](end_span)
a_careful_approach_to_warning_signs.useful_question: “Is this a brief difference, or is it a persistent pattern that affects the child’s everyday participation, learning, communication, safety, comfort, or wellbeing?[span_117](start_span)”[span_117](end_span)

A_physical_and_motor_development.overview: Physical and motor development includes large movements, small hand movements, balance, strength, coordination, posture, and daily physical functioning.[span_118](start_span)[span_118](end_span)
gross_motor_skills: Crawling, scooting, or moving around in another way[span_121](start_span)[span_121](end_span)
gross_motor_patterns_worth_discussing: Very little spontaneous movement or exploration over time.[span_127](start_span)[span_127](end_span)
Persistent stiffness, unusual floppiness, weakness, or a clear difference between the two sides of the body.[span_128](start_span)[span_128](end_span)
Persistent difficulty sitting, standing, walking, or moving around compared with expected development.[span_129](start_span)[span_129](end_span)
Persistent falling, poor balance, or coordination that limits ordinary play.[span_130](start_span)[span_130](end_span)
A new or sudden change in walking, balance, strength, or movement.[span_131](start_span)[span_131](end_span)
A child who stops doing a movement skill they had previously mastered.[span_132](start_span)[span_132](end_span)
Pain, distress, or avoidance connected to movement.[span_133](start_span)[span_133](end_span)
Difficulty with movement that significantly affects eating, dressing, play, toileting, or participation.[span_134](start_span)[span_134](end_span)
fine_motor_skills: Moving objects from one hand to the other[span_136](start_span)[span_136](end_span)
Picking up small safe items with fingers[span_137](start_span)[span_137](end_span)
Dressing tasks such as pulling off loose clothing[span_142](start_span)[span_142](end_span)
fine_motor_patterns_worth_discussing: Persistent difficulty using both hands together during play or daily tasks.[span_144](start_span)[span_144](end_span)
A noticeable difference in hand use or strength.[span_145](start_span)[span_145](end_span)
Difficulty grasping, releasing, manipulating, or using everyday objects.[span_146](start_span)[span_146](end_span)
Fine motor difficulties that significantly interfere with feeding, dressing, play, drawing, or self-care.[span_147](start_span)[span_147](end_span)
Loss of hand skills that were previously present.[span_148](start_span)[span_148](end_span)
age_appropriate_motor_examples: By age 2, most children can kick a ball, run, walk up a few stairs with or without help, and eat with a spoon.[span_149](start_span)[span_149](end_span)

By 30 months, many children can jump with both feet leaving the ground, turn book pages one at a time, use hands to twist objects, and take off some clothing.[span_150](start_span)[span_150](end_span)
By age 3, many children can put on some loose clothing, use a fork, and draw a circle after seeing an example.[span_151](start_span)[span_151](end_span)

B_language_and_communication.overview: Communication includes much more than spoken words. Children may communicate through: Eye gaze, Facial expression, Sounds, Crying, Body movements, Gestures, Pointing, Showing objects, Reaching, Signs, Pictures, Speech, Words in one or more languages, Communication devices, where used.[span_152](start_span)[span_152](end_span)
understanding_language_patterns_worth_di: Responding to familiar words, sounds, or voices.[span_153](start_span)[span_153](end_span)
Recognising common objects or people when named.[span_155](start_span)[span_155](end_span)
Participating in familiar songs, stories, play routines, or group activities because they do not seem to understand what is happening.[span_157](start_span)[span_157](end_span)
expressing_language_patterns_worth_discu: Very limited use of gestures, sounds, signs, words, pictures, or other ways to communicate.[span_158](start_span)[span_158](end_span)
Persistent difficulty communicating basic needs or interests.[span_159](start_span)[span_159](end_span)
Little progress in adding new communication skills over time.[span_160](start_span)[span_160](end_span)
Marked frustration because the child cannot make themselves understood.[span_161](start_span)[span_161](end_span)
Speech that is persistently very difficult for familiar adults to understand as the child grows.[span_162](start_span)[span_162](end_span)
Loss of words, gestures, sounds, or communication skills that were previously used.[span_163](start_span)[span_163](end_span)
social_communication_patterns_worth_disc: Limited attempts to share interest, enjoyment, or attention with familiar adults.[span_164](start_span)[span_164](end_span)
Rare use of gestures to request help, show something, or share interest.[span_165](start_span)[span_165](end_span)
Limited response to name or familiar voices, especially when hearing is also a concern.[span_166](start_span)[span_166](end_span)
Difficulty joining familiar social routines or games.[span_167](start_span)[span_167](end_span)
Reduced back-and-forth interaction compared with the child’s own previous development.[span_168](start_span)[span_168](end_span)
age_appropriate_communication_examples: By age 2, most children: Point to things in a book when asked. Say at least two words together, such as “more milk.” Point to at least two body parts when asked. Use gestures beyond waving and pointing, such as nodding “yes” or blowing a kiss.[span_169](start_span)[span_169](end_span)
By 30 months, many children say about 50 words, combine two or more words including an action word, name pictures in books, and follow two-step instructions.[span_170](start_span)[span_170](end_span)
By age 3, many children use at least two back-and-forth conversational exchanges and ask simple questions.[span_171](start_span)[span_171](end_span)

C_cognitive_development.overview: Cognitive development includes how children learn, explore, remember, solve simple problems, understand routines, and adapt to new situations. Young children do not need to sit still for long periods, complete formal academic tasks early, or learn at exactly the same speed as other children.[span_172](start_span)[span_172](end_span)
patterns_worth_discussing: Very limited exploration or interest in people, objects, or activities over time.[span_173](start_span)[span_173](end_span)
Persistent difficulty learning familiar routines despite repeated, supportive teaching.[span_174](start_span)[span_174](end_span)
Difficulty understanding simple concepts or solving simple everyday problems in ways that affect participation.[span_175](start_span)[span_175](end_span)
Attention or memory difficulties that consistently interfere with learning, play, safety, or daily activities.[span_176](start_span)[span_176](end_span)
A marked loss of skills in play, understanding, memory, or problem-solving.[span_177](start_span)[span_177](end_span)
Concerns across several areas, rather than one isolated task.[span_178](start_span)[span_178](end_span)

D_social_and_emotional_development.overview: Social and emotional development includes relationships, feelings, comfort, play, regulation, confidence, and participation with others.[span_179](start_span)[span_179](end_span)
patterns_worth_discussing: Persistent difficulty connecting with familiar caregivers or accepting comfort when distressed.[span_180](start_span)[span_180](end_span)
A marked change in social engagement or emotional expression.[span_181](start_span)[span_181](end_span)
Persistent distress, fearfulness, withdrawal, or difficulty regulating emotions that significantly limits ordinary activities.[span_182](start_span)[span_182](end_span)
Ongoing difficulty participating in play, routines, or relationships across settings.[span_183](start_span)[span_183](end_span)
Loss of social behaviours or interaction skills that were previously present.[span_184](start_span)[span_184](end_span)
A combination of social, communication, and play concerns that continues over time.[span_185](start_span)[span_185](end_span)

what_is_developmental_regression.definition: Developmental regression means that a child loses a skill they had already gained and used consistently.[span_187](start_span)[span_187](end_span)
examples: A child who previously used several words but stops using them.[span_188](start_span)[span_188](end_span)
A child who previously waved, pointed, or used gestures but no longer does so.[span_189](start_span)[span_189](end_span)
A child who previously walked steadily but now has difficulty walking.[span_190](start_span)[span_190](end_span)
A child who previously fed themselves but can no longer manage a skill they had mastered.[span_191](start_span)[span_191](end_span)
A child who previously joined familiar songs, games, or interactions but has stopped doing so.[span_192](start_span)[span_192](end_span)
A child who becomes markedly less responsive or less engaged than before.[span_193](start_span)[span_193](end_span)
what_is_developmental_regression.note: Regression is different from slow progress. Slow progress means a child is gaining skills more slowly than expected. Regression means a child appears to lose skills they already had.[span_194](start_span)[span_194](end_span)

why_regression_needs_prompt_attention.explanation: Loss of skills deserves prompt professional discussion because it can have many possible causes, including health, neurological, sensory, emotional, environmental, or developmental factors. It is not possible to identify the cause simply by watching a child or searching online.[span_195](start_span)[span_195](end_span)

regression_versus_temporary_changes.explanation: Children may temporarily seem quieter, more clingy, less independent, or less communicative when they are: Ill, Tired, Recovering from a hospital stay, Starting childcare or school, Adjusting to a move, bereavement, separation, or new sibling, Experiencing major changes in routine, Under stress.[span_196](start_span)[span_196](end_span)
regression_versus_temporary_changes.note: However, if a child has truly stopped using skills they previously used regularly, if the loss persists, or if you are uncertain, do not wait and try to decide the cause yourself. Encourage the parent or caregiver to speak to a qualified healthcare professional promptly.[span_197](start_span)[span_197](end_span)

what_caregivers_should_do: Write down the skills the child used before and what has changed.[span_199](start_span)[span_199](end_span)
Note when the change began and whether it was sudden or gradual.[span_200](start_span)[span_200](end_span)
Record any relevant illness, injury, medication change, stressful event, or hearing/vision concern.[span_201](start_span)[span_201](end_span)

Seek urgent medical care immediately if regression is accompanied by serious illness, seizures, sudden weakness, a new major walking problem, loss of consciousness, severe headache, repeated vomiting, breathing difficulty, or another acute medical concern.[span_203](start_span)[span_203](end_span)

why_combinations_matter.overview: One isolated difference may reflect normal variation. However, a pattern involving more than one developmental area may be more significant and deserves a fuller professional discussion.[span_205](start_span)[span_205](end_span)

examples_of_concern_patterns.pattern_observed: Limited spoken communication + limited gestures + difficulty understanding familiar instructions[span_206](start_span)[span_206](end_span)
examples_of_concern_patterns.why_a_fuller_discussion_may_help: Communication should be considered broadly, including hearing, understanding, gesture use, language exposure, and social interaction[span_207](start_span)[span_207](end_span)

examples_of_concern_patterns.pattern_observed: Motor difficulty + trouble with feeding, dressing, or ordinary play[span_208](start_span)[span_208](end_span)
examples_of_concern_patterns.why_a_fuller_discussion_may_help: A professional can consider strength, coordination, pain, opportunity to practise, health, and functional impact[span_209](start_span)[span_209](end_span)

examples_of_concern_patterns.pattern_observed: Difficulty learning routines + difficulty following instructions + persistent concern at home and childcare[span_210](start_span)[span_210](end_span)
examples_of_concern_patterns.why_a_fuller_discussion_may_help: A fuller picture can explore language, hearing, attention, sleep, health, learning opportunities, and daily functioning[span_211](start_span)[span_211](end_span)

examples_of_concern_patterns.pattern_observed: Limited social engagement + communication concerns + loss of previously used skills[span_212](start_span)[span_212](end_span)
examples_of_concern_patterns.why_a_fuller_discussion_may_help: This should be discussed promptly with a healthcare professional; learners should not attempt to identify the cause[span_213](start_span)[span_213](end_span)

examples_of_concern_patterns.pattern_observed: Frequent falls + apparent weakness + reduced participation in play[span_214](start_span)[span_214](end_span)
examples_of_concern_patterns.why_a_fuller_discussion_may_help: The pattern should be discussed with a healthcare professional, especially if it is new, worsening, or affecting safety[span_215](start_span)[span_215](end_span)

examples_of_concern_patterns.pattern_observed: Speech concern + poor response to sounds + repeated ear problems[span_216](start_span)[span_216](end_span)
examples_of_concern_patterns.why_a_fuller_discussion_may_help: Hearing assessment may be important, alongside broader communication assessment[span_217](start_span)[span_217](end_span)

whole_child_questions: Is the child making progress, staying the same, or losing skills?[span_221](start_span)[span_221](end_span)
Does this occur at home and in childcare or school?[span_222](start_span)[span_222](end_span)
Are there concerns about hearing, vision, sleep, nutrition, illness, pain, or behaviour?[span_223](start_span)[span_223](end_span)
Does the child understand and communicate differently in different languages or environments?[span_224](start_span)[span_224](end_span)

development_is_influenced_by_many_factor: Hearing: Hearing difficulties can affect speech, language, attention, learning, and social participation.[span_227](start_span)[span_227](end_span)
Vision: Vision difficulties can affect movement, play, learning, safety, and interaction.[span_228](start_span)[span_228](end_span)
Nutrition: Adequate nutrition supports growth, energy, health, and learning.[span_229](start_span)[span_229](end_span)
Sleep: Poor or insufficient sleep can affect mood, attention, behaviour, learning, and participation.[span_230](start_span)[span_230](end_span)
Chronic illness: Some health conditions can affect energy, attendance, hearing, movement, or learning.[span_231](start_span)[span_231](end_span)
Recurrent illness: Frequent illness may temporarily affect progress or participation.[span_232](start_span)[span_232](end_span)
Premature birth: Children born early may need development interpreted using corrected age in the early years, as advised by their healthcare team.[span_233](start_span)[span_233](end_span)
Pain or discomfort: Ear pain, dental pain, constipation, breathing problems, or other discomfort can affect behaviour and participation.[span_234](start_span)[span_234](end_span)
Opportunities for play and learning: Children need safe opportunities to move, explore, communicate, imitate, play, and practise skills.[span_235](start_span)[span_235](end_span)
Responsive caregiving: Warm, responsive interactions support communication, emotional security, and learning.[span_236](start_span)[span_236](end_span)
Language environment: Children may use more than one language or communication method, and assessment should consider the whole communication environment.[span_237](start_span)[span_237](end_span)
Psychosocial stress: Family hardship, violence, displacement, caregiver distress, loss, or major instability can affect wellbeing and development.[span_238](start_span)[span_238](end_span)
Environmental conditions: Safety, overcrowding, access to play space, pollution, and community resources may influence children’s opportunities and health.[span_239](start_span)[span_239](end_span)

hearing_and_vision_assessments.overview: Hearing and vision are especially important to consider when there are concerns about communication, learning, attention, play, or movement.[span_240](start_span)[span_240](end_span)
hearing_and_vision_assessments.important_note: Important: Do not assume that a hearing, vision, sleep, nutrition, or environmental issue explains every developmental concern. These factors are part of the whole picture that professionals may explore.[span_241](start_span)[span_241](end_span)

developmental_monitoring.definition: Developmental monitoring is the ongoing process of noticing how a child develops over time.[span_243](start_span)[span_243](end_span)
includes: Skills that are not emerging as expected[span_248](start_span)[span_248](end_span)
Skills that appear to have been lost[span_249](start_span)[span_249](end_span)
Factors that help or make participation harder[span_250](start_span)[span_250](end_span)

developmental_screening.definition: Developmental screening uses a standardised and validated tool to identify children who may need further evaluation or support.[span_251](start_span)[span_251](end_span)
developmental_screening.note: A screening tool cannot diagnose a child. It can show that further discussion, observation, assessment, or referral may be helpful.[span_252](start_span)[span_252](end_span)

professional_assessment.definition: A professional developmental assessment is more detailed than monitoring or screening.[span_253](start_span)[span_253](end_span)
professional_assessment.goal: The goal is not simply to name a condition. The goal is to understand the child’s strengths, needs, functioning, and the support that may help.[span_254](start_span)[span_254](end_span)

key_distinctions.question: Is it ongoing?[span_255](start_span)[span_255](end_span)
key_distinctions.screening: Usually a specific time point or concern-triggered event[span_257](start_span)[span_257](end_span)

key_distinctions.question: Does it diagnose?[span_267](start_span)[span_267](end_span)
key_distinctions.professional_assessment: It may contribute to diagnosis when performed by qualified professionals[span_270](start_span)[span_270](end_span)

key_distinctions.question: What is the main purpose?[span_271](start_span)[span_271](end_span)
key_distinctions.screening: Identify whether further evaluation may be needed[span_273](start_span)[span_273](end_span)
key_distinctions.professional_assessment: Understand the child comprehensively and plan support[span_274](start_span)[span_274](end_span)

sections.important_professional_guidance: The AAP recommends developmental surveillance at every routine health supervision visit, developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months, and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months. Concerns raised at other times should also prompt screening or referral as appropriate.[span_275](start_span)[span_275](end_span)

lessons.title: What Should a Parent or Caregiver Do?[span_276](start_span)[span_276](end_span)

a_practical_response_stay_calm_and_act_e: Stay calm. A concern does not equal a diagnosis. Avoid panic, blame, or assumptions.[span_277](start_span)[span_277](end_span)
Observe carefully. Notice what the child can do, what is difficult, and when the concern appears.[span_278](start_span)[span_278](end_span)
Document specific examples. Record what happened, when, where, and what support helped.[span_279](start_span)[span_279](end_span)

Consider age and context. Think about illness, sleep, hearing, vision, language exposure, recent changes, opportunities to practise, and whether the child was born prematurely.[span_280](start_span)[span_280](end_span)
Look for patterns over time. Is the concern persistent? Is progress continuing? Is the child losing skills? Is the concern present in more than one setting?[span_281](start_span)[span_281](end_span)
Talk with the parent or primary caregiver if appropriate. Use a respectful, strengths-based approach. Share observations, not labels.[span_282](start_span)[span_282](end_span)

Discuss the concern with a qualified healthcare professional. This may be a child health clinic, primary healthcare provider, doctor, nurse, paediatrician, developmental professional, or another appropriate local service.[span_283](start_span)[span_283](end_span)
Ask about screening, hearing and vision checks, or assessment if recommended. Follow local referral pathways.[span_284](start_span)[span_284](end_span)

Continue supporting the child while waiting. Keep talking, playing, reading, singing, using routines, offering movement opportunities, and responding warmly to the child’s communication attempts.[span_285](start_span)[span_285](end_span)
Follow up. Attend appointments, share records, ask what the next step is, and continue observing progress.[span_286](start_span)[span_286](end_span)
guidance_for_teachers_and_childcare_work: Speak privately with the parent or caregiver.[span_288](start_span)[span_288](end_span)
Avoid making diagnoses or suggesting a specific condition.[span_291](start_span)[span_291](end_span)
Ask what the family sees at home.[span_292](start_span)[span_292](end_span)
Encourage consultation with an appropriate healthcare professional when concerns persist or are significant.[span_293](start_span)[span_293](end_span)
Keep information confidential and share it only with authorised people who need it to support the child.[span_294](start_span)[span_294](end_span)
Follow the organisation’s safeguarding, referral, and record-keeping procedures.[span_295](start_span)[span_295](end_span)
sections.example_respectful_conversation_with_a_p: “I enjoy seeing how Ama likes songs and watches the other children during group time. Over the last month, I have noticed that she uses very few words here and often becomes frustrated when she cannot show us what she wants. She does use pointing and brings adults to objects. I would like to understand what you see at home and whether you have noticed anything similar. It may be helpful to discuss her communication and hearing with her healthcare provider. This is not a diagnosis—it is a way to make sure she gets any support she may need.[span_296](start_span)”[span_296](end_span)

useful_information_to_share: The child’s age and date of birth.[span_298](start_span)[span_298](end_span)
Whether the child was born prematurely, if relevant.[span_299](start_span)[span_299](end_span)
Whether the concern is improving, staying the same, worsening, or changing.[span_303](start_span)[span_303](end_span)
Whether the behaviour occurs at home, childcare, school, or other settings.[span_304](start_span)[span_304](end_span)
Any concerns about hearing, vision, sleep, eating, feeding, pain, illness, or medication.[span_308](start_span)[span_308](end_span)
Relevant medical history, such as recurrent ear infections or chronic illness.[span_309](start_span)[span_309](end_span)
Notes, videos, reports, or examples from home or childcare, where appropriate and with consent.[span_310](start_span)[span_310](end_span)

good_communication_versus_alarming_commu.clear_useful_language: “I am concerned because my child is 2½ and uses only a few spoken words. I would like advice about their communication development.[span_312](start_span)”[span_312](end_span)
“She uses few words and does not often point to show us things. Can we discuss whether she needs developmental screening or assessment?[span_314](start_span)”[span_314](end_span)
“He often does not respond when called, especially in noisy places, and he has had several ear infections. Could hearing be checked?[span_316](start_span)”[span_316](end_span)
“She needs repeated support to follow familiar two-step instructions and this happens at home and childcare. What could be affecting this?[span_318](start_span)”[span_318](end_span)
“He used to say ‘mama,’ ‘ball,’ and ‘bye-bye’ daily. Over the past six weeks, he has stopped using these words. I would like prompt advice.[span_320](start_span)”[span_320](end_span)

sections.goal: The goal is to describe the child’s experience accurately and respectfully, not to persuade a professional that a particular diagnosis is correct.[span_321](start_span)[span_321](end_span)

sections.the_development_concern_pathway: NOTICE → OBSERVE → DOCUMENT → DISCUSS → SEEK GUIDANCE → FOLLOW UP[span_323](start_span)[span_323](end_span)

steps.action: Notice a change, a missed skill, a persistent difficulty, or a concern raised by a parent, caregiver, teacher, or another adult.[span_325](start_span)[span_325](end_span)
steps.questions: What exactly have I noticed? Is this new? Is it affecting the child’s daily life? What strengths do I also see?[span_326](start_span)[span_326](end_span)

steps.action: Observe across ordinary activities and, where possible, across more than one day or setting.[span_328](start_span)[span_328](end_span)
steps.areas_to_look_at: Communication, Movement, Play and learning, Social interaction, Emotional regulation, Daily routines, Hearing and vision responses, Health and wellbeing.[span_329](start_span)[span_329](end_span)

steps.action: Write down facts: What happened? When and where? What did the child do? What support helped? What skills does the child already have? Has the child lost any skills?[span_331](start_span)[span_331](end_span)
Speak respectfully with the parent or caregiver. Invite their perspective.[span_333](start_span)[span_333](end_span)

Encourage contact with an appropriate healthcare or developmental professional when a concern is persistent, significant, involves more than one area, affects participation, or includes possible regression.[span_335](start_span)[span_335](end_span)

Continue supportive daily interactions. Ask whether the family received guidance, what support is in place, and whether additional observations would be useful.[span_337](start_span)[span_337](end_span)

practical_guidance_by_situation.suggested_learner_response: Observe respectfully over a short, defined period; offer normal developmental support; document examples; discuss with the parent/caregiver; encourage routine professional discussion if concern continues[span_339](start_span)[span_339](end_span)
Encourage professional discussion rather than continuing to “wait and see” without a plan; share objective observations[span_341](start_span)[span_341](end_span)
Encourage a more comprehensive professional review; consider hearing, vision, health, and whole-child development[span_343](start_span)[span_343](end_span)
Encourage prompt professional assessment; document the lost skills and timing; do not try to determine the cause[span_345](start_span)[span_345](end_span)

practical_guidance_by_situation.situation: Sudden new weakness, new walking difficulty, seizures, loss of consciousness, severe illness, breathing difficulty, severe headache with vomiting, or other acute symptoms[span_346](start_span)[span_346](end_span)
practical_guidance_by_situation.suggested_learner_response: Seek urgent medical care using local emergency procedures; this is beyond routine developmental monitoring[span_347](start_span)[span_347](end_span)

sections.important_note: Important: This is an educational framework, not a medical triage system. Follow local emergency and referral procedures, and seek qualified medical advice when there is a serious or sudden concern.[span_348](start_span)[span_348](end_span)

mistakes_table.why_it_is_unhelpful: A learner cannot diagnose from observation, checklists, or internet searches[span_351](start_span)[span_351](end_span)
Terms such as “lazy,” “naughty,” “slow,” or “antisocial” can stigmatise and hide the real issue[span_354](start_span)[span_354](end_span)

mistakes_table.why_it_is_unhelpful: Children develop at different rates and may need time, practice, or support[span_360](start_span)[span_360](end_span)
mistakes_table.better_approach: Look for patterns, context, persistence, and functional impact[span_361](start_span)[span_361](end_span)

case_study.title: Case study: “He will talk when he is ready[span_386](start_span)”[span_386](end_span)
case_study.child_info: Child: Tunde. Age: 2½ years. Setting: Home and community childcare programme.[span_387](start_span)[span_387](end_span)
case_study.background: Tunde lives with his mother, father, older sister, and grandmother. His family speaks Yoruba and English at home. He attends a community childcare programme three mornings each week. Tunde’s mother says that he understands some familiar routines. He brings his shoes when the family says it is time to go out. He enjoys watching his sister play with toy cars. He smiles during songs and laughs when adults play chase games. However, Tunde uses very few spoken words. His family regularly hears “mama,” “no,” and “car,” but he does not often put words together. When he wants juice, he may pull an adult toward the kitchen or cry. At childcare, he often takes an adult’s hand to a shelf instead of pointing or using words.[span_388](start_span)[span_388](end_span)
case_study.context: Some relatives say, “Do not worry. Boys talk late. Children develop at different speeds.” Tunde had several ear infections during the previous year. His mother says he sometimes seems not to respond when someone calls him from another room, although he responds quickly when he hears a favourite song or when someone opens a packet of biscuits. His childcare worker has not noticed concerns about his running, climbing, or using toys. He enjoys rolling cars, stacking blocks, and looking at picture books with an adult. There is no known loss of words or other skills; his mother says he has always used only a small number of words.[span_389](start_span)[span_389](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 1. Could this be normal variation?[span_390](start_span)[span_390](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: Yes, some variation in language development is normal. Some children begin speaking later than others, especially when they are otherwise making steady progress in communication, understanding, gestures, play, and social interaction. However, normal variation should not be used as a reason to ignore a persistent concern. At 2½ years, very limited spoken language deserves discussion with a qualified healthcare professional, especially when the child uses only a few words and is not regularly combining words. The correct conclusion is not “Tunde definitely has a disorder” and not “there is definitely nothing to discuss.” The correct conclusion is: “Tunde’s communication development needs a closer look.[span_391](start_span)”[span_391](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 2. What additional information would be useful?[span_392](start_span)[span_392](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: Useful questions include: How many words does Tunde use across Yoruba and English combined? Does he use gestures such as pointing, waving, nodding, showing objects, or reaching to request help? Does he point to share interest, not only to request something? Does he understand familiar words and simple instructions in Yoruba, English, or both? Does he respond to his name in quiet settings? Does he respond to everyday sounds? Does he use eye contact, facial expression, sound, gesture, or play to communicate? Does he take turns in simple games? Does he imitate words, sounds, actions, or household tasks? Does he communicate differently at home and childcare? Has he had frequent ear infections, ear pain, blocked ears, or other hearing concerns? Has he lost any words, gestures, social behaviours, or motor skills? Are there concerns about sleep, feeding, health, or other developmental areas? What happens when adults pause and wait for him to communicate? What communication strategies help him most?[span_393](start_span)[span_393](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 3. What should be observed?[span_394](start_span)[span_394](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: Adults could observe: Spoken words in both languages. Sounds, gestures, pointing, leading adults by the hand, showing objects, and facial expressions. Understanding of one-step and two-step familiar instructions. Response to name, voices, and sounds in quiet and noisy settings. Joint attention: whether he looks at an adult and an object to share interest. Play skills: imitation, pretend play, use of toys, and enjoyment of interaction. Frustration during communication. Interaction with familiar adults and other children. Progress over several weeks.[span_395](start_span)[span_395](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 4. Could hearing be relevant?[span_396](start_span)[span_396](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: Yes. Tunde’s history of ear infections and inconsistent response to being called make hearing an important factor to discuss. Responding to favourite sounds does not prove that a child hears all speech sounds clearly, especially in noisy settings. A healthcare professional may recommend a hearing assessment as part of understanding his communication development. This does not mean hearing is definitely the cause. It is one important factor to consider.[span_397](start_span)[span_397](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 5. Is there evidence of regression?[span_398](start_span)[span_398](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: No regression is described. Tunde has not lost words or other skills he previously used consistently. His concern is limited language progress, not loss of skills. This is important because loss of previously acquired skills would require more prompt professional attention.[span_399](start_span)[span_399](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 6. Are there concerns in other developmental areas?[span_400](start_span)[span_400](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: The available information suggests strengths in movement, play, enjoyment of songs, picture books, and interaction with familiar adults. More information is still needed about understanding language, gesture use, social communication, hearing, and participation in routines.[span_401](start_span)[span_401](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 7. What should the caregiver do next?[span_402](start_span)[span_402](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: Record clear examples of Tunde’s communication in Yoruba and English. Note his gestures, understanding, responses to sound, and frustrations. Discuss the concern with his healthcare provider or child health clinic. Mention his previous ear infections and inconsistent response to name. Ask whether hearing assessment, developmental screening, speech-language support, or further assessment is appropriate. Continue supporting communication at home and childcare: Talk during daily routines. Follow his interests in play. Use simple words and short phrases. Pause and wait for him to respond. Respond positively to gestures and sounds. Read picture books together. Use gestures, objects, pictures, or choices to support understanding and expression. Avoid pressuring him to repeat words or shaming him for not speaking.[span_403](start_span)[span_403](end_span)

guided_discussion.question: 8. Why is self-diagnosis inappropriate?[span_404](start_span)[span_404](end_span)
guided_discussion.answer: Many different factors can affect communication, including hearing, language exposure, individual variation, understanding of language, speech development, broader developmental differences, health, and opportunities for interaction. Tunde’s relatives, caregiver, and teacher cannot determine the cause from his number of spoken words alone. Professional assessment is needed to understand the whole picture. Key learning point: Tunde does not need a label from his family or caregiver. He needs respectful observation, a hearing and developmental discussion with qualified professionals, and supportive communication experiences every day.[span_405](start_span)[span_405](end_span)

practical_activity.title: Activity: From Observation to Appropriate Action[span_406](start_span)[span_406](end_span)
practical_activity.instructions: Read each scenario. For each one, answer: What was observed? What additional information is needed? What should be monitored or documented? When should professional guidance be considered? What should the adult avoid saying or doing? Do not diagnose the child. Use respectful, objective language.[span_407](start_span)[span_407](end_span)

scenarios.scenario_title: Scenario 1: A child who is quiet in a new setting[span_408](start_span)[span_408](end_span)
scenarios.description: Amina is 20 months old and has started attending a neighbour-led childcare group two weeks ago. She stays close to her aunt at drop-off, watches the other children, and cries when her aunt leaves. She speaks very little at the childcare group, but her aunt says Amina uses several words at home, points to ask for things, enjoys songs, and follows simple everyday instructions. By the end of each session, Amina sometimes smiles and rolls a ball back and forth with one caregiver.[span_409](start_span)[span_409](end_span)

analysis.what_was_observed: Amina is cautious and distressed during a recent transition to a new childcare setting. She uses less spoken language there than at home but shows some engagement by the end of sessions.[span_410](start_span)[span_410](end_span)
analysis.what_more_is_needed: Ask how long the adjustment has been occurring, how Amina communicates at home, whether she understands routines, whether she gradually becomes more comfortable, and whether there are concerns in other settings.[span_411](start_span)[span_411](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_monitored: Separation distress, gradual comfort with familiar caregivers, play, gesture use, communication attempts, and participation over several weeks.[span_412](start_span)[span_412](end_span)
analysis.when_should_guidance_be_considered: If distress remains intense and persistent, if she is unable to participate over time, if communication concerns also occur at home, or if there are broader concerns.[span_413](start_span)[span_413](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_avoided: Avoid saying “She is antisocial,” “She has anxiety,” or “She cannot speak.” Do not force her to separate abruptly or shame her for crying.[span_414](start_span)[span_414](end_span)
analysis.rationale: A new childcare setting can be stressful. The available information includes reassuring strengths: words at home, gestures, understanding, songs, and gradual engagement. This scenario calls for supportive monitoring, not diagnosis.[span_415](start_span)[span_415](end_span)

scenarios.description: Kofi is 28 months old. His father says Kofi says “mama,” “ball,” and “go,” but rarely uses other words. He points sometimes but often cries or pulls adults by the hand when he wants something. His preschool teacher says he enjoys playing with blocks and cars but does not consistently respond when called from across the room. He has had several episodes of ear pain in the past year.[span_417](start_span)[span_417](end_span)

analysis.what_was_observed: Kofi uses a small number of spoken words, communicates through behaviour and leading adults, and may not consistently respond to voice. There is a history of ear pain.[span_418](start_span)[span_418](end_span)
analysis.what_more_is_needed: Ask about all languages used at home, understanding of familiar instructions, gestures, social interaction, response to sounds in quiet settings, ear infections, hearing history, play, and whether any skills were lost.[span_419](start_span)[span_419](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_monitored: Communication attempts, word growth, gestures, understanding, response to sound, frustration, and differences between home and preschool.[span_420](start_span)[span_420](end_span)
analysis.when_should_guidance_be_considered: Professional guidance should be sought now because the concern is persistent, communication is limited, and hearing may be relevant.[span_421](start_span)[span_421](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_avoided: Avoid saying “He is stubborn,” “He is deaf,” “He has autism,” or “Boys always talk late, so wait.[span_422](start_span)”[span_422](end_span)
analysis.rationale: This scenario does not identify a diagnosis. It supports a healthcare discussion that includes hearing assessment and developmental communication review.[span_423](start_span)[span_423](end_span)

scenarios.scenario_title: Scenario 3: A child who has stopped using words[span_424](start_span)[span_424](end_span)
scenarios.description: Lebo is 30 months old. Her mother reports that Lebo previously used around 15 words, including names of family members and favourite foods. Over the last two months, she has stopped using most of these words. She now mainly cries, hums, and takes adults by the hand. Her grandmother says this began after Lebo had a fever, but Lebo is now physically well. She still runs, climbs, and enjoys being held by her mother.[span_425](start_span)[span_425](end_span)

analysis.what_was_observed: Lebo appears to have lost words she previously used consistently. This may be developmental regression in communication.[span_426](start_span)[span_426](end_span)
analysis.what_more_is_needed: Clarify which words were used, when they stopped, whether gestures or social interaction have changed, whether there were seizures or other illness symptoms, whether hearing seems different, and whether any other skills have changed.[span_427](start_span)[span_427](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_monitored: Exact words lost, communication methods now used, response to sound, social engagement, play, eating, sleep, illness symptoms, and other skill changes.[span_428](start_span)[span_428](end_span)
analysis.when_should_guidance_be_considered: Prompt professional assessment should be encouraged because loss of previously acquired communication skills needs timely attention.[span_429](start_span)[span_429](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_avoided: Avoid waiting for months, assuming she is “just being difficult,” blaming the family, or deciding what caused the regression.[span_430](start_span)[span_430](end_span)
analysis.rationale: Loss of previously acquired skills requires prompt professional discussion. The learner’s job is to document and support referral, not determine the cause.[span_431](start_span)[span_431](end_span)

scenarios.scenario_title: Scenario 4: Difficulty with movement and daily activities[span_432](start_span)[span_432](end_span)
scenarios.description: Chiamaka is 4 years old. Her teacher notices that she avoids running games, falls more often than other children during outdoor play, and struggles to climb low steps without holding tightly to an adult. At lunch, she can feed herself but takes much longer than peers to open containers or use a spoon without spilling. Her father says, “She has always been a careful child.” Her teacher has noticed the pattern for four months.[span_433](start_span)[span_433](end_span)

analysis.what_was_observed: Chiamaka has persistent difficulty with balance, movement, and some hand-use tasks that may affect participation in play and meals.[span_434](start_span)[span_434](end_span)
analysis.what_more_is_needed: Ask about development over time, whether she has pain, weakness, tiredness, recent illness or injury, vision concerns, movement at home, history of falls, and whether skills are improving or worsening.[span_435](start_span)[span_435](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_monitored: Specific movement tasks, balance, falls, fatigue, hand use, pain, supports that help, and whether difficulties occur across settings.[span_436](start_span)[span_436](end_span)
analysis.when_should_guidance_be_considered: Professional guidance should be encouraged because concerns are persistent, affect daily activities, and occur in more than one functional area.[span_437](start_span)[span_437](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_avoided: Avoid saying “She is lazy,” “She is clumsy,” or “She has a motor disorder.” Do not force participation in activities that feel unsafe.[span_438](start_span)[span_438](end_span)
analysis.rationale: Caution can be a temperament trait, but the persistent pattern and impact on participation make this appropriate for professional discussion.[span_439](start_span)[span_439](end_span)

scenarios.description: Said is 4½ years old. At home, his family speaks Somali. At preschool, the main language is English. His teacher says he rarely answers questions in English and often watches other children before joining an activity. His older brother says Said tells long stories at home in Somali and enjoys pretend play with cousins. The teacher has not yet spoken to the family about the languages used at home.[span_441](start_span)[span_441](end_span)

analysis.what_was_observed: Said may have limited confidence or language understanding in English at preschool, while reportedly communicating strongly in Somali at home.[span_442](start_span)[span_442](end_span)
analysis.what_more_is_needed: Ask about his communication skills in Somali, exposure to English, how long he has attended preschool, whether he understands visual demonstrations, and whether concerns appear in both languages.[span_443](start_span)[span_443](end_span)
analysis.what_should_be_monitored: Participation over time, nonverbal communication, play, understanding with visual support, progress in English exposure, and communication across languages.[span_444](start_span)[span_444](end_span)
